newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu decrees emergency, rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu decrees emergency, rebels advance.

text.p: Zaire's embattled president Mobutu Sese Seko decreed a nationwide state of emergency in the face of a relentless advance by rebel forces controlling a third of the central African country.

A senior U.S. official said the veteran leader's time had passed and that the key question was how he chose to relinquish power after dominating the sprawling and corruption-plagued country for over three decades.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said members of Mobutu's elite presidential guard were putting up a fight on the approaches to Zaire's southern second city Lubumbashi. The guard themselves said they had pushed back rebels there.

"We are meeting stiff resistance in Lubumbashi but it is something we expected," Kabila told reporters in the newly captured diamond city Mbuji-Mayi. "We are moving in many columns so they don't know what is coming after the first salvo."
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 but has seen his hold over the sprawling country crumble as the rebels advance, announced the emergency via a decree on state television.
It said a state of emergency declared in the eastern provinces of North and South Kivu last October "is extended throughout the national territory".
It said five military governors had been appointed in provinces not held by the rebels, who took up arms in October vowing to topple Mobutu.
Mobutu's decree did not make clear what restrictions would be imposed under the state of emergency or the implications for Kinshasa and its more than five million people.

In Washington, the State Department's "Mr Africa" George Moose told a congressional hearing that Mobutu and his regime were "a thing of the past" but that the nature of the transition to a "post-Mobutu scene" was important.
"How he departs the scene is important. Mr Mobutu could play a positive role," the U.S. assistant secretary of state told a House International Affairs subcommittee hearing.
Mobutu returned to Kinshasa on March 21 from cancer treatment in Europe. He had prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland in August.
Zaire's new Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi, facing stiff political opposition after less than a week in the job, would formally move into his offices on Wednesday, state radio said.
Tshisekedi has alienated Mobutu's allies and even his own opposition backers by excluding all but his most loyal followers from a cabinet he announced on his first day in power last week.
His militant supporters have staged protests in Kinshasa to block efforts by the two sides in parliament to oust him from the job.
Representatives of Kabila and of Mobutu wrapped up four days of talks in South Africa on Tuesday with a statement recognising the need for talks on a peaceful solution and a truce.
The statement did not make clear how or when a ceasefire might be implemented. Each side was departing for consultations.

On the humanitarian front, the U.N. refugee agency pressed on with a plan to airlift 100,000 exhausted Rwandan Hutu refugees home from the war zone. Spokesman Paul Stromberg said preparations could take 10 days.
